text: Ida Fiyo Mntwana (1903 – March 1960) was a South African anti-apartheid and women's rights activist. She worked as a dressmaker and became politically active in the 1950s. After Madie Hall Xuma resigned as national president of the African National Congress Women's League (ANCWL) in 1949, Mntwana succeeded her and was more radical, organizing women in demonstrations, strikes, and other acts of civil disobedience. She was elected to the African National Congress (ANC) executive committee. In 1954, Mntwana became the first president of the Federation of South African Women (FEDSAW) and helped organize the Congress of the People. On the second day of the congress, police invaded the event and created a conflict between the people and the police; it was Mntwana who calmed the crowd by singing a freedom song from the platform, ensuring the congress continued. On 26 August 1952, she led a march in Germiston consisting of 29 women: 11 Indian, one Coloured (Susan Naude), and 17 African women. She and the group were detained and sentenced to fourteen days in Boksburg prison. She also led the FEDSAW march to the Union Buildings in Pretoria on 27 October 1955, with around 2,000 women participating to protest pass laws for women. Mntwana was one of the defendants in the 1956 Treason Trial and died in March 1960 during this trial. She is represented in one of 100 bronze statues as part of the National Heritage Monument's project, The Long March to Freedom, with her statue created by Sarah Lovejoy. In August 2000, Mntwana was cited as "torchbearer" during Thabo Mbeki's speech at the unveiling of South Africa's Women's Monument. She was awarded a posthumous Order for Meritorious Service in silver in 2003.
